edges.title: Liszt and Grieg’s Piano Concerto, Rome, 1870

works.from: Liszt’s letter of 29 December 1868 and his sight-reading in Rome, 1870
works.to: Violin Sonata No. 1 in F major, Op. 8; Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16 (manuscript)

edges.claim: On 29 December 1868 [[liszt]] wrote from Rome to a young Norwegian he had never met, praising his F major Violin Sonata and inviting him to Weimar. Grieg had not sent it. When they met in Rome in 1870, Liszt took the manuscript of the Piano Concerto, played it straight through at the keyboard, talking and nodding as he went, and handed it back with the words: “you have what it takes, and don’t let them frighten you.” His testimonial had already helped Grieg win a state travel grant.

sources.title: Henry T. Finck, Edvard Grieg (John Lane, 1906)
sources.locator: pp. 31–37: Liszt’s letter of 29 December 1868, Grieg’s letter to his parents about the 1870 meetings, and the government grant

sources.title: Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon: Edvard Grieg
sources.locator: Liszt’s 1868 letter; the 1869 stipend granted on Liszt’s testimonial; two meetings in Rome in 1870, when Liszt played the concerto at sight

edges.title: Tchaikovsky’s Hamlet overture, dedicated to Grieg

works.to: Grieg’s letters to Tchaikovsky of April and May 1888

edges.claim: On 1 January 1888 [[tchaikovsky]] met Grieg and his wife Nina at the Leipzig home of the violinist Adolph Brodsky; after dinner Nina sang her husband’s songs. Tchaikovsky first meant to dedicate his Fifth Symphony to Grieg. He went on to write the Hamlet fantasy-overture that summer and inscribed it “à Edvard Grieg”. Grieg had written to him in May: “Kindred spirits don’t grow on trees!”

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Edvard Grieg
sources.locator: Tchaikovsky and Grieg (Leipzig, 1 January 1888 N.S.; Grieg’s letters of 12 April and 26 May 1888); Dedications (Fifth Symphony intended, Hamlet, Op. 67 inscribed)

edges.title: Grieg’s Piano Concerto after Schumann’s

works.from: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 54
works.to: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16

edges.claim: Grieg’s only piano concerto, drafted at Søllerød in the summer of 1868, is in the same key as [[schumann]]’s A minor concerto. Like Schumann’s, it opens with a flourish for the soloist and has no long orchestral exposition before the piano enters. In Leipzig Grieg had heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto, and half a century later he wrote in his diary that every tempo of her performance stayed stamped on his soul.
edges.note: Grieg’s own remark that he studied the Schumann concerto before writing his is reported in a programme note, and Finn Benestad writes that it was probably his model, above all for the first movement. No letter by Grieg naming the model has been consulted.

sources.title: Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon: Edvard Grieg
sources.locator: Clara Schumann’s performance of the concerto and the diary entry; the concerto composed at Søllerød; Schumann’s concerto probably the model for the first movement

sources.title: Laurie Shulman, New Jersey Symphony programme note on Grieg’s Piano Concerto (2019)
sources.locator: Grieg’s concerto compared with Schumann’s: same key, opening flourish for the soloist, no double exposition

edges.title: Grieg at the first Bayreuth Festival, 1876

works.from: Der Ring des Nibelungen, first Bayreuth Festival, 1876

edges.claim: In the summer of 1876 Grieg was at Bayreuth for the opening of the first festival, where [[wagner]]’s Ring was staged complete for the first time. He sent eight long reports to the Bergen newspaper Bergensposten. As a student in Leipzig he had already seen Tannhäuser fourteen times.

sources.title: Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon: Edvard Grieg
sources.locator: Leipzig years (Tannhäuser seen fourteen times); summer 1876, Bayreuth and the eight reports in Bergensposten
